page.title: Other systems
page.description: Send events to actors in other processes and machines: a function you write carries each message, and the other host takes it unchanged.

hero.headline: Send events to actors in other processes
hero.lede: An actor sends to an actor on another machine by its address. A function you write carries the message, and the other side's host takes it unchanged, a Python host included.

section.heading: Give each host a system name
section.p: The system option names a host's system, and every address starts with it: tinyactors://<system>/.... Actors of one system reach actors of another, in this process or on another machine, by address.
The host delivers a send to its own system's address itself. A send to any other system goes to your transport option, a handler that carries it there.
You choose the wire and its encoding. The other side gives each message to its host with host.send (Wire format).

section.heading: Send to an actor by its address
section.p: actor.address gives an actor's address, and host.actor(address) finds the actor a local address names.
host.send takes an Actor, a session, an address string or an Address. On the host named shop, tinyactors://shop/@teller reaches the actor spawned with the name teller.
A message's origin is the sender's address as the other side gave it. The receiving actor reads it as _event.origin.

section.heading: Carry each send to the other host
section.p: The transport handler gets each send to another system as a Send. The other side passes its send.message to host.send(message) as it is.

item.text: The outgoing half: target, event, data, sendid, origin and traceparent, null for a field the send lacks. A Python host's host.send takes it too.
The receiver's and the sender's addresses, as Address values.
Write the message as CBOR, its addresses as CBOR's tag 32, as a Python host's encode does, and read them back as Address values.

section.p: Here two hosts in one process pass encoded messages through a timer. The shop's checkout asks the bank's teller for a charge, and the teller approves it.

example.code: charging 12 for tinyactors://shop/#_scxml_1 approved by tinyactors://bank/#_scxml_1

section.p: The teller answers to _event.origin, the checkout's full address, so the approval goes back through the bank's transport.

section.heading: Connect two processes over TCP
section.p: Between processes, the transport writes each message as a frame on a connection: four bytes of length, then the message's CBOR.
Call socket.setNoDelay(true) on both ends. Node.js turns on Nagle's algorithm by default, which holds a second small write until the peer acknowledges the first.
That wait is about 40 ms on Linux's loopback, and an answer is often a second small frame. Python's asyncio turns the algorithm off by itself.
In this program the bank listens on a port and the shop connects. The charge and the approval cross the connection as one frame each.

section.heading: Tell the sender when delivery fails
section.p: When the transport cannot write a frame, or the peer is gone, it calls send.fail() while its handler runs. After the handler has returned, call host.fail(sender, sendid) on the sending host.
There sender is the message's origin, the actor that sent it, not the target it was for. That actor gets error.communication with that sendid.
Only a failure needs a call: a delivered send needs nothing more. A host without a transport handler fails every send to another system.

section.heading: Read an address into its parts
section.p: new Address(text) reads an address into its system, session (a bigint) and name, each undefined when the text lacks it.
Address.fromSession(system, session) and Address.fromName(system, name) make one, and toString() gives its text. This program makes both kinds and reads text that is no address.

example.code: tinyactors://shop/#_scxml_42 shop 42n tinyactors://shop/@front%20desk front desk undefined

section.heading: Write messages as JSON
section.p: JSON.stringify writes each address of a send.message as its text (address.toJSON()). The other side's host.send takes the parsed message, its addresses as strings, and new Address(text) reads one back.
Inside event data an address is plain text: values have no address type.

section.heading: Read and write BasicHTTP requests
section.p: SCXML defines BasicHTTP, a way to send events as HTTP form posts. The package writes and reads those requests, for an I/O processor or a server of your own.

item.text: Writes the request a send makes, as bytes for a socket.
Reads an incoming request's form fields and its event: the _scxmleventname field, or HTTP.<METHOD>.

example.code: POST /scxml HTTP/1.1 POST /scxml order.placed sku=tea qty=2

section.p: The host hands each send to your I/O processor, and your program writes the bytes and serves the port.
